extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and news professionals (reporters, editors)
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-1940s Associated Press style collection of wartime dispatches, human-interest stories, and feature reporting covering military training, battle developments, and correspondent performance. The page mixes frontline news, organizational reporting, and descriptive feature writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful and comprehensive reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The great stories of the war have been told graphically, truthfully and comprehensively by the greates[t] array of reportorial eye-witnesses...' (Kent Cooper lauding A.P. correspondents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report accuracy and completeness are primary standards. Examples: eyewitness, diary, or correspondent dispatches that convey facts and context. Anti-pattern: allowing propaganda or unverified claims to substitute for factual, comprehensive accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness constrained by military necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting should be as swift as possible but delays are sometimes 'understandably due to military or naval necessities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable to delay publication when security or operational concerns require it. Scoring note: timeliness is valued but subordinate to operational security; explain delays when possible to maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of reportorial/photographic enterprise as safety permits
rubrics_metrics.description: There have been 'no unreasonable restrictions on the assignments of war correspondents or camera men ... as freely as military security or due regard for their own safety permits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for wide-ranging reporting and photography but respect constraints imposed by military/security authorities. Anti-pattern: claiming unrestricted access when censorship/security prevented coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid, continuous training program structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The course takes 60 days. There are no days off. Every Monday a new class enters, and every Monday a class graduates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design training for continuous throughput: fixed-length intensive cycles, weekly intake/graduation cadence. Example metrics: 60-day total course, zero days off, weekly class turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive specialization in training
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of 30 days for each class, records are reviewed and the last 30 days the men concentrate on their special jobs (command of a large ship, gunnery officer, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a two-phase curriculum: initial common foundation followed by role-specific specialization. Evaluate and place trainees on merit after the common phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful selection and weeding of trainees
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘You'll do nothing of the sort. I'll pick my own.' ... 'I've got some dregs here. Get them out.' 'A man who'll quit on a school book will quit in battle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should select candidates they trust and remove poor performers early. Anti-pattern: accepting large numbers without screening and retaining persistently slow or unfit trainees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harsh discipline and psychological conditioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Student officers get tougher treatment... 'McDaniels wants those men especially, because they arrive fully equipped with the hatred they need for the job ahead.' 'It was held that a man who'll quit on a school book will quit in battle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training emphasizes toughness, strict discipline, and cultivating the mindset needed for combat roles. Warning: this is a historical practice described here; modern ethical standards differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, hands-on instruction and sea training
rubrics_metrics.description: Training concentrates on 'intricate instruments which detect the presence and movement of a submarine' and 'train at sea' so men learn to handle their ships and instruments in real conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize experiential learning on the actual platforms and equipment. Use survivors and experienced seamen as instructors. Anti-pattern: purely classroom-based instruction without real-world practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of survivors and experienced personnel as instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Key men from ships at sea are returned here both to study and teach. The student personnel also includes many survivors of ships. McDaniels wants those men especially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate frontline survivors and experienced practitioners into the instructor cadre to transfer tacit knowledge and combat-tested techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingual instruction for allied trainees
rubrics_metrics.description: Men from almost every allied nation have studied here... 'They're all taught in their own language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide instruction in trainees' native languages to maximize comprehension and effectiveness when training international/cooperating forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal formal text; use concise, practical course materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The school still has no text-books; but it has a mimeographed outline of courses to keep the instructors from overlapping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer compact, practical course outlines (e.g., mimeographed guides) over heavy textbooks to allow rapid updates and focused training. Anti-pattern: over-reliance on voluminous theory when speed and adaptability are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational graduation and immediate assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Things move so fast at the school there is no ceremony when a class graduates. They merely line up, and get their orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduation is measured by operational readiness; graduates are immediately assigned where needed rather than ceremonial recognition. Metric: post-graduation deployment within days of completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resourcefulness and rapid scaling of facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: He’s taken over nine hotels ... a chow hall overflow eats in two more places appropriated by McDaniel: an auto show room, and a former restaurant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scaling training rapidly, repurpose available civilian facilities (hotels, showrooms, restaurants) to meet housing, feeding, and classroom needs. Example: improvising sleeping/feeding spaces when piers or barracks lack capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative practicality over red tape
rubrics_metrics.description: He’s practically free of red-tape for the simple reason that he writes practically no letters. There isn’t time. He either uses the phone, or takes the steps personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor direct communication (phone, in-person) and minimal paperwork to accelerate decisions in urgent programs. Anti-pattern: excessive bureaucracy that delays critical operational actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid medical evacuation and transfer to general hospitals
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Our ambulances meet the planes, one of which sometimes carries as many as fifteen wounded, and in a very brief time the patients are under our care. This naturally improves their chances of recovery, as a general hospital has facilities which could not be maintained in the field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize quick transfer from front/airfield to well-equipped general hospitals to improve recovery; coordinate ambulance/airlift rendezvous to minimize time-to-care.
